Motivation / Background

We have two ways to configure things that get filtered in logs: filter_parameters and filter_attributes. The latter was added in 2018 and ensures that things added to filter_parameters are also added to filter attributes. However, the opposite is not true, which makes for some weird behavior right out of the box.

Take this example with a model called CreditCard with two attributes: digits and cvv.

cvv is added to filter_parameters by default:

digits is added to filter_attributes:

Which results in logs that look like this:

Detail

This PR aims to ensure that if you've added something to filter_attributes, it is filtered by default in the logs.

Additional information

I looked at several places to put this code. I don't love where it is now, but we do have a circular loading problem because the AR classes get loaded well after filter_parameters are precompiled.

items.content_html:
Parse dates in "YYYY-MM-DD" format with a regex, falling back to Date.parse.

Implementation uses a proc-local match-data variable to be threadsafe (instead of using globals $1, $2, and $3).

This fixes a longstanding TODO, added by @jeremy in October 2007. Let's fix this TODO before it's old enough to vote, buy a lottery ticket, and get a face tattoo!

Here is a micro-benchmark that demonstrates the performance improvement in the typical case, when the regex matches:

require "benchmark/ips"
require "date"

DATE_STR = "2025-06-25"
DATE_REGEX = /\A(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})\z/

def parse_with_regex
  m = DATE_REGEX.match(DATE_STR)
  Date.new(m[1].to_i, m[2].to_i, m[3].to_i)
end

def parse_with_date_parse
  Date.parse(DATE_STR)
end

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.config(time: 5, warmup: 2)

  x.report('Regex + Date.new') { parse_with_regex }
  x.report('Date.parse')       { parse_with_date_parse }

  x.compare!
end

Here is the output of the benchmark on my laptop:

ruby 3.4.4 (2025-05-14 revision a38531fd3f) +PRISM [arm64-darwin24]
Warming up --------------------------------------
    Regex + Date.new   175.876k i/100ms
          Date.parse    60.591k i/100ms
Calculating -------------------------------------
    Regex + Date.new      1.775M (± 0.5%) i/s  (563.43 ns/i) -      8.970M in   5.053946s
          Date.parse    607.273k (± 0.3%) i/s    (1.65 μs/i) -      3.090M in   5.088588s

Comparison:
    Regex + Date.new:  1774838.2 i/s
          Date.parse:   607272.8 i/s - 2.92x  slower

items.content_html:
Overview

This patch adds the ability to deprecate associations:

has_many :posts, deprecated: true

With that, Active Record will report any usage of the posts association.

Modes

There are two deprecation modes, :warn and :notify.

In :warn mode, usage issues a warning using ActiveRecord::Base.logger (normally, same as Rails.logger in Rails applications). The message includes some context and the application-level place where the access happened, if any. This is the default mode.

In :raise mode, usage raises an ActiveRecord::DeprecatedAssociationError with a similar message.

In :notify mode, usage publishes a deprecated_association.active_record Active Support notification. The payload has the association reflection (:reflection), the application-level location (:location) where the access happened (a Thread::Backtrace::Location object, or nil), and a deprecation message (:message).

Use cases

The main use case for this feature is deleting an association. By deprecating first, you can identify and eliminate current usage before the actual removal.

Even if the test suite reports no usage, you can still monitor production in case there is mocked usage or lack of coverage for whatever reason.

The :notify mode is particularly flexible. You can use it to register usage in a structured manner, thanks to the objects in the payload. It can also be used in creative ways, like enabling the flag dynamically for all associations and introspecting usage in CI, which can help detect unused associations in your code base. Subscribers may have arbitrary logic, allow lists per team, bubble up things only once, create CI artifacts, etc.

Configuration

In Rails applications, the mode is set with the new configuration parameter config.active_record.deprecated_associations_mode, which is :warn by default.

What is Considered to be Association Usage

Associations API

The entire associations API is guarded, think Author#posts, Author#posts=, Author#post_ids, etc.

Nested Through Associations

By following throughs and sources, a through association may be chained arbitrarily deep.

Say a through association has other 7 nested ones, and let's assume 2 of them are deprecated. Every usage of the root through association reports those 2, since they are used, even if only to generate JOINs.

Nested Attributes

If there is also

accepts_nested_attributes_for :posts

Any assignment via posts_attributes= is reported.

Queries

For example, in queries like

Author.includes(:posts).where(...)

Side Effects

An association may have side effects.

For example, if a deprecated has_many has dependent: :nullify, FKs become NULL whenever the owner is destroyed, and that would stop happening if you remove the association (you remove the association, not necessarily the database table or other associations pointing to that table). Because of that, a warning is issued if the owner is destroyed, and the context explains why (see next section).

Deprecation Context

In order to help users understand the reported deprecated usage, each deprecation message has additional context.

Some examples:

  • The association Author#posts is deprecated, the method post_ids was invoked
  • The association Appointment#patients is deprecated, referenced as nested association of the through Physician#patients
  • The association Author#posts is deprecated, referenced in query to preload records
  • The association Author#posts is deprecated, :dependent has a side effect here
  • ...

The Implementation

Association Builders

  • Association builders accept a new :deprecated option.
  • They add guards to the generated APIs.
  • Guards go via association.reflection to have the reflection validated.
  • They may add callbacks to cover implicit usage via side effects.

Association Reflections

  • Association reflections respond to deprecated?.
  • Through associations respond to deprecated_nested_reflections, which is a cached array of nested deprecated association reflections (possibly empty).

Queries

By guarding in the precise places when preloading or joining, I believe all is covered. Please let me know if something is overlooked.

ActiveRecord::Associations::Deprecation

The core of the feature is centralized in the new private module ActiveRecord::Associations::Deprecation

Testing

The models/dats directory has stripped-down versions of existing fixture models. I tried first to add new deprecated associations in the existing models, but became too complicated due to side effects. With these ad-hoc models we have much more control.

Documentation Comes Next

Once feedback is addressed, I'd like to merge and followup with documentation in API and guides.

Thanks

I wrote a simpler version of this feature for @Gusto, we are collaborating together. This was initially a private monkey patch to Active Record that is helping them identify and refactor associations that cross certain boundaries.

After seeing its potential, @Gusto decided to contribute this work back, so all Rails users can benefit from it. This has been also done in the context of our collaboration.

Would like to thank @Gusto on behalf of the Rails community for this.
items.title: Deprecated Associations

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Closes #51044
Supersedes #51045
Addresses #51045 (comment)

Detail

Deprecates providing boolean and nil (where explicitly supported) arguments to the following relation query methods:

  • #lock
  • #readonly
  • #strict_loading
  • #distinct

By extension, the changes to #lock will also affect the following model methods:

  • #lock!
  • #with_lock

In the case of true or nil, all that is needed to address the deprecation is omit the argument. In the case of false, I've introduced new #unscope_<query_method> methods which users can migrate to instead.

Additional information

Some or all of these methods may have unintentionally accepted truthy and falsy values as arguments, which creates ambiguity—one of the key motivations behind these changes. Considering none of these behaviours have been documented or tested against, neither the deprecation message nor the changelog entry refer to them.

I've only changed public APIs in these changes. All these methods call out to undocumented relation query methods (e.g. #lock!) that actually mutate the relation, and those in turn may be relying on similar arel methods, both of which may and will continue to handle truthy/falsy arguments.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because it's increasingly necessary to create complex DOM identifiers and the existing dom_id is limited.

This PR creates a new method ActionView::RecordIdentifier#dom_target that can create a unique identifier from an unlimited number of objects, which differentiates it from dom_id which only takes a single object and an optional string prefix.

dom_target(Post.find(45))                  # => "post_45"
dom_target(Post.find(45), :edit)           # => "post_45_edit"
dom_target(Post.find(45), :edit, :special) # => "post_45_edit_special"
dom_target(Post.find(45), Comment.find(1)) # => "post_45_comment_1"

I chose the name of target because I found myself wanting this for generating turbo-rails Turbo Broadcast targets. dom_target is inspired by the structure of turbo_stream_from(*streamables), which concatenates an unlimited number of objects into a single identifier.

Adding an new helper method is proposed as an alternative to adding new behavior to existing dom_id or dom_class helper methods, which had questions/objections. Related:

  • #44081
  • #50608
  • hotwired/turbo-rails#543

Motivation / Background

The Turbo::Broadcastable#broadcasting_to API allows you to specify composite channels. Here is an example:

class DocumentSuggestion < ApplicationModel
  belongs_to :document
  broadcasts_refreshes_to -> { [ it.document, it.document.owner ] }
end

This has really useful utility for a lot of use cases. It would be good if ActionCable::Channel#stream_for had similar ergonomics.

This Pull Request has been created because I believe it is likely others will find this a nice API to use and likely even expected by others (I did at least).

I do understand that using Turbo::Streams is likely a good solution for most ActionCable use cases but there are definitely use cases where piping data instead of HTML still makes sense – e.g. Using ActionCable to facilitate WebRTC signalling.

Detail

This Pull Request changes ActionCable::Channel::Broadcasting#stream_for to allow passing multiple models similar to Turbo::Broadcastable#broadcasting_to works.

class BroadcastSignalChannel < ApplicationCable::Channel
  def subscribed
    return reject unless set_account_broadcast

    stream_for [ @account_broadcast, current_user ]
  end
  
  #...
end

Additional information

I have updated the test suite to include cases covering the enhancements to the API.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Ref #55161

In Rails 7, a new render tracking implementation was added to Rails: the RipperTracker. From that commit message:

Using a parser finds dependencies that would otherwise be difficult to
find with the regular expressions. It should also theoretically work
with other template systems since it operates on the compiled template
instead of the contents of the file.

It was initially made the default render tracker, but that change was later backed out.

Since then, the Prism parser was released and made the default Ruby parser. A Prism render tracker implementation was also added to Rails in 7.2.

Detail

Until now, there hasn't been a "blessed" way for applications to try out the new tracker implementations (you would have to go through private API). This commit adds configuration to not only make it easy for applications to use the new Ruby-parser-based trackers, but it also makes these new trackers the default for new applications on 8.1.

The new trackers are not only better at finding render calls, they are also much easier to maintain. When I added trailing interpolation tracking to the three trackers, the Prism tracker was by far the easiest to work with.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because Rails was appending ; charset=utf-8 to pure JSON responses (Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8), which contradicts the IANA registration for application/json (no charset parameter defined). Nik Clayton reported this in issue #55063 and we need to align Rails’ behavior with the spec.

This pull request needs to be merged because:

  • Bug fix: Corrects non-spec-compliant behavior in JSON APIs so that consumers see exactly Content-Type: application/json. Fixes #55063
  • Interoperability: Some HTTP frameworks and clients strictly parse Content-Type parameters; removing the charset prevents subtle bugs or middleware rejections.
  • Consistency with MDN and IANA: Aligns Rails with widely-cited documentation (MDN) and the official media-type registration.
  • User impact: Applications serving JSON via Rails APIs will immediately benefit and no longer need manual workarounds.

Detail

This Pull Request changes:

  • Overrides ActionDispatch::Response#content_type= so that when the MIME type is exactly application/json, Rails uses set_content_type 'application/json', nil instead of defaulting to UTF-8.
  • Leaves all other content types unchanged, preserving existing charset logic.

Additional information
